section.title: The Decision Problem of a Theory
section.para: A theory T is a set of sentences closed under logical consequence in some fixed logical framework. The decision problem of T asks whether there exists a finite, effective method that, given any sentence φ in the language of T, determines in finitely many steps whether φ is or is not a theorem of T.
Tarski stated the criterion as follows:

blockquote.para: A theory T is called decidable if there exists a method by means of which, for every sentence φ formulated in the terms of T, it can be decided in a finite number of steps whether φ is or is not provable (i.e., derivable) in T; otherwise T is called undecidable.
blockquote.attribution: Alfred Tarski, Andrzej Mostowski, and Raphael M. Robinson, Undecidable Theories, North-Holland, 1953, p. 3.

section.para: The phrase a method by means of which — equivalently, Tarski's earlier phrasing proved by means of the devices available in T — calls for formal precision. What counts as a device? What counts as a method? These questions are addressed in the sections that follow.
